en: The Rhapsody on the Three Robes from the "Rhapsody on the Requisites of the Great Wise Vinaya Master":
I possess the three robes, the true regulations of the ancient sages. Coarse and sparse hemp and ramie constitute their substance; [the use of] animal fur and silkworm silk would cause harm.
Life is harmed by [the wearing of] blue-black and madder-dyed robes, which destroy its natural color.
While the five primary and five secondary colors may provoke worldly censure regarding their observance, these robes are like the two wings of a bird and like the thin skin that protects the body.

They are the banner of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the model for the conduct of noble Śramaṇas, and the foremost sign for those of the ninety-six paths who give rise to faith. Twenty.
Fifth, there is the foundation for planting merit: thus, the King of Beasts (the Lion) made a firm vow and endured death while repeatedly offering praise;
the Lotus-Colored Woman engaged in play yet completely severed greed and delusion. Their great vows were most profound and their sublime virtues inconceivable.

The dragon was spared from the calamity of the golden-winged bird, and people obtained relief from the peril of warring enemies. Yet in these later times, customs have become frivolous and superficial, and the True Teaching has declined.
Competing to sell disordered robes of vermilion, you ultimately met with the ridicule of those who play false flutes; you grew arrogant and conceited, oppressing those of great virtue and hoary hair.
This became a habitual custom, and in your folly you did not recognize your error. You should now reverently follow the eternal norms and look up with gratitude for the grace bestowed upon you.
Rejoice at every moment, never depart from this path even for a single step, and let your spirit dwell in the Land of Bliss, where your tenuous garments shall naturally [ascend].
Though this world-system of Jambudvīpa may be suspended and the kalpas of the eternal stone may wear away, these words shall not vanish;
though the great void may come to an end, it is certain that this resolve shall never be moved.
An Essay on the Iron Almsbowl:
I possess an iron bowl, its craftsmanship perfectly executed; half a *dou* in capacity, it is neither too large nor too small.
Treated by the smoke of bamboo, it is resplendent and pure—resembling a bright pearl divided in two, or like the full moon about to become perfect. At dawn, I enter the village.
The multitude of hearts surged forth as the yellow millet was scattered and dispersed, like golden sand and white rice husks;
the high mounds resembled accumulated snow, no different from the miraculous manifestations of the Gandha-vyūha Heaven, and no distinction from the natural celestial offerings.

I address you, my fellow voyagers: you must each reflect upon yourselves. Without plowing, without grain, without weeding, and without harvesting, from what source shall the lives of living beings be sustained?
Furthermore, the mouth and belly know no satiety; the source of greed is inexhaustible. If right mindfulness falters even slightly, the rākṣasa has already seized you.

To indulge in the sweet flavors of a single moment is to suffer hunger and thirst for ten thousand kalpas. One may accept ten thousand pieces of gold, provided they are preserved until the meal is finished;

yet a mere cup of water is difficult to endure if one lacks restraint. The Holy Teachings clearly explain this: one should not violate the five reflections and must observe moderation with the three spoonfuls. Be careful not to wrong others.
One accepts the offerings of the faithful to sustain this defiled body, yet one must rely on these necessary conditions to seek early liberation for oneself.
Regarding the sitting mat:
I have been granted a sitting mat, and its dimensions are well-established; as for its color and appearance, it is of the same category as the *kāṣāya*, and as for its substance...
Two layers of coarse cloth, four spans long and three wide; when worn out, fold the new over the old. Since its form is large, it may be opened and expanded.

My body is small, yet from the beginning the regulations favored the large and loathed the small. Thus one blames others for their faults while turning the regulations into a pretext for expansion—how could one know that one is deceiving oneself?
I have heard that the bhikṣu’s body is a five-part stūpa, and the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is...
This is the foundation of the four quarters; thus, the Way is that upon which one relies. How could it be appropriate to protect only the body?

When practicing dhyāna or expounding the Dharma, spread [the teachings] without failing in dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*); when entering villages or traveling through the regions, maintain [this practice] without straying even a single step.

Otherwise, there will be violations of the various precepts and the imposition of disciplinary penalties, such that for one's entire life there will be no opportunity to sit in accordance with the Dharma.
The Preface to the Water-Strainer:
I possess a water-strainer, crafted with skillful method; fine silk forms its base, and tempered iron constitutes its frame. When using it for filtration, one must observe closely;
when returning it to its case, one must take care not to damage it. One should know that even our Buddha’s benevolence and compassion do not...

Leaving behind these minor matters, we shall ensure that our descendants may drink [the Dharma] and fortunately escape further calamity. Within a single realm of transformation, both superiors and inferiors are governed;
within half a *yojana*, one must travel back and forth. Yet the world mostly treats this with negligence—few investigate its merits or flaws.
Some hear of it but do not establish it, deriding it as a "lesser vehicle" (*hīnayāna*); others establish it but do not practice it, merely hanging it in their thatched huts.
Because you lack internal compassion while externally indulging in negligence— blocking the paths for those who seek refuge and obstructing the fundamental principles of my teaching—
you must maintain sincerity and guard [the Dharma], exerting all your strength to restore and expand it. This will not only provide reliance for the four modes of birth,
but shall also cause the Three Jewels to increase in glory.

**Rhapsody on the Śikya Staff** I possess a śikya staff, fashioned according to the prescribed form. Its three sections are equal in length, its trunk rises six feet high, and it is encircled by twelve rings, complete and without flaw.
It demonstrates the conditions of cause and effect—how there is death and how there is birth. The two prongs open and yet remain joined, manifesting both emptiness and existence.
It is detached from the world yet not withdrawn; it does not support the weak, but merely seeks alms. When held, it remains utterly silent; when shaken, its cry rings out clearly.
It truly desires to open the gates of all realms of existence and to still the sufferings of the three miserable paths. Wherever it rests, it should be hung upon the walls of one’s dwelling;
though dust and grime easily accumulate, it must be wiped clean. To cast it beyond the clouds is no hardship for it.
To contend with the tiger requires no small effort; how fortunate that the common and ignorant may tread upon the traces of the Sage!
Though they manifest coarseness and violence outwardly and harbor thorns within, if they can employ this [teaching] and let it go, will they not be free from evening anxieties?
